rv.q: Jamie Lloyd delivers an effortlessly deft revival of Lucy Prebble’s play, set during the clinical trial of a new antidepressant

This puts the emphasis on divisions within the black community rather than on race. Demure, ballet-trained psychology student Connie is matched with talkative wide boy Tristan; posh, patrician Toby, son of a surgeon, faces hardscrabble Lorna, who scornfully explains that, as a black woman, getting out of bed in the morning is a political act.

On either side of the traverse stage sit Dr Lorna James (Michele Austin, utterly captivating), the experiment’s psychologist, and Dr Toby Sealey (Kobna Holdbrook-Smith, his voice like velvet), the boss who needs the trial to work.

The play’s central question is a grabby one. Cocky Hackney drifter Tristan and sceptical Canadian psychology student Connie join the clinical trial for cash, but end up in love instead. Are their feelings real, or is it just artificial dopamine that’s giving them the heart eyes?

For The Effect needs to primarily convince as a love story as well as make us question the extent to which feelings, even existence itself, can be quantified. As Tristan and Connie, Paapa Essiedu and Taylor Russell are a joy to watch, Essiedu’s clumsy charismatic libido beautifully bumping up against Taylor’s slowly melting analytical reserve.

That worrying bucket contains a human brain, which both doctors address like gatecrashers at Yorick’s autopsy: it is Austin’s Dr James, however, who sticks the scalpel right into the play’s soft amygdala when she reveals how cruelly this solid lump talks to her, pushing her towards the edge.

Firecracker director Jamie Lloyd is never one to do things by half measures. The Lyttelton, the National’s most awkward auditorium, has been reconfigured into a sleek traverse staging, on which the four actors pulse and prowl, at times resembling caged animals in a zoo, at others prize fighters limbering up for an epic bout.

Tristan is a charmer from Hackney; Connie a thoughtful, inward-looking psychology student from Canada. They meet in a double-blind clinical trial for antidepressants and fall in love. But as they upset the trial with their amorous antics, they also wonder whether their love is real or a by-product of the drugs.
